Sanctions screening: how to review a hit

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 6, 2026•7 min read

Sanctions screening compares customers, counterparties and transactions against the sanctions lists published by OFAC, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, so that a bank or fintech can block or reject what sanctions prohibit. The stakes are set by how OFAC enforces: its 2021 ransomware advisory notes that "OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations based on strict liability", which means a firm can be liable even when it did not know it was dealing with a sanctioned party.

This guide covers what screening has to catch, what OFAC expects from a screening program, the six steps OFAC recommends for reviewing a potential match, and what three recent enforcement cases say about where screening fails. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What screening has to catch

The main list is the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (the SDN List). OFAC also publishes non-SDN lists with different prohibitions, including the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications (SSI) List, the Foreign Sanctions Evaders (FSE) List and the Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions (NS-MBS) List. These are combined in OFAC's Consolidated list. The chart in OFAC's FAQ 5 puts parties on the SDN List under blocking, while certain activities with parties on some non-SDN lists call for rejecting the transaction instead. The review has to know which list it hit.

Screening also has to cover programs that target whole jurisdictions or governments. FAQ 5 gives Iran and the Government of Cuba as examples. That means looking at countries and addresses and, for online services, IP locations, which figure in two of the enforcement cases below.

OFAC's 50 Percent Rule adds another layer. Any entity owned "in the aggregate, directly or indirectly, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons" is itself blocked, "regardless of whether the entity itself is listed". OFAC's FAQs on the rule add that it "speaks only to ownership and not to control", and that holdings of people blocked under different programs are added together. Screening names alone will not find these entities. You need ownership information from KYB and beneficial ownership checks as well.

What OFAC expects from a screening program

OFAC's Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments (May 2019) describes a sanctions compliance program in five parts: "(1) management commitment; (2) risk assessment; (3) internal controls; (4) testing and auditing; and (5) training." In the Framework, screening tools come up under internal controls, and testing and auditing checks them. The Framework expects that an organization "has selected and calibrated the solutions in a manner that is appropriate to address the organization's risk profile and compliance needs", and that it "routinely tests the solutions to ensure effectiveness." A program should also be "capable of adjusting rapidly to changes published by OFAC".

The Framework lists common root causes of violations. One of them is "Sanctions Screening Software or Filter Faults", which covers firms that:

  • "failed to update their sanctions screening software to incorporate updates to the SDN List or SSI List";
  • "failed to include pertinent identifiers such as SWIFT Business Identifier Codes";
  • "did not account for alternative spellings of prohibited countries or parties", with examples such as Habana for Havana and Kuba for Cuba.

OFAC's FAQs do not name a required product or a match threshold. FAQ 27 calls the question "primarily a question for your regulator" and says an adequate program depends on who your customers are and what business you do, and FAQ 28 says "The frequency of running an OFAC scan must be guided by your organization's internal policies and procedures."

How to review a potential match: OFAC's six steps

OFAC FAQ 5, last updated September 9, 2026, sets out the steps it recommends for deciding whether an alert is a valid match:

  1. Find out which list the alert hit. Screening tools often include non-OFAC lists, such as the Commerce Department's Entity List. If the hit is on another agency's list, contact that agency; OFAC does not advise on matches unrelated to its sanctions.
  2. Find out what kind of OFAC nexus it is. A name on an OFAC list goes to step 3. A jurisdiction, a government, or an unlisted entity blocked under the 50 Percent Rule should be escalated to a supervisor or the compliance team before anything is processed.
  3. Judge the quality of the match. Pull the full list entry and compare it with what you hold: date of birth, nationality, ID and registration numbers, addresses, aliases. OFAC notes that many alerts are false positives and that an address match alone may not be enough. If you "can reasonably determine the match is not valid", you may proceed.
  4. Handle a likely match. If several details match and nothing rules the person out, follow your procedures for likely matches and check whether a general or specific license authorizes the activity.
  5. Block or reject. "If OFAC sanctions require blocking, you must freeze the assets or property". If the activity is prohibited but no blocked person has an interest in it, the transaction must be rejected.
  6. Report and keep records. Blocked property and rejected transactions must be reported to OFAC within 10 business days, under 31 CFR 501.603 and 501.604.

Two more points from the same FAQ are worth building into procedures. OFAC "does not confirm potential matches or false positives", so the decision is yours to make and document. And organizations "should keep complete, accurate records detailing the steps taken to investigate the potential match and the information relied upon".

What a disposition record should hold

Based on those expectations, a cleared or escalated alert should leave a record that a tester or examiner can follow without asking the analyst:

  • the alert, the list it hit and the list entry as it stood on the day of review;
  • the customer or transaction data compared, and where each item came from;
  • the identifiers that matched and the ones that ruled the match out;
  • the decision, the reason in plain words, the reviewer and the time;
  • any escalation, license check, block or rejection, and the report reference if one was filed.

The same record also supports the PEP and adverse media reviews that often run on the same customer.

What recent enforcement cases show

OFAC's enforcement releases describe what went wrong in detail. Three recent ones turn on screening:

CasePenaltyScreening problems OFAC described
Bank of America, N.A. (October 13, 2026)$11,662,930Payments processed before the screening filter was updated after a designation; a watchlist that went un-updated for about five weeks in 2023 because of a vendor error; exact name and date-of-birth matches ranked as low or medium priority; an alert suppression rule that released payments; payments identified as false positives and approved for processing.
TradeStation Securities (March 17, 2026)$1,110,661An IP geo-blocking layer left disabled after a software update, a dropped automated test tool, and a vendor alert subscription that lapsed for more than eight months.
Interactive Brokers (July 15, 2025)$11,832,136An alert "incorrectly dispositioned" as a false positive, Crimea missing from the IP blocking list, and a delay in getting the ownership information needed to apply the 50 Percent Rule.

Several of these failures followed a change: a new designation, a software release, a vendor problem or a move to a new screening platform. The TradeStation release warns against a "set it and forget it" approach, and the Bank of America release states that "Each organization remains responsible for its own compliance regardless of whether it relies upon third-party providers."

In practice that means testing screening after every list update, software release, vendor change and platform migration; giving exact name and date-of-birth matches the highest priority; and keeping a written escalation path for likely matches.

How long to keep the records

In April 2024, Public Law 118-50 extended the statute of limitations for violations of the main sanctions statutes, IEEPA and TWEA, from five years to 10. OFAC then extended its recordkeeping requirement to match, in a rule that took effect in March 2025. 31 CFR 501.601 now requires records to be kept "for at least 10 years after the date of such transaction". Separately, blocked property held on June 30 has to be reported every year by September 30.

Common questions

Does OFAC require specific screening software?

No. OFAC calls it primarily a question for your regulator. The Framework does expect the tool to be calibrated to your risk profile and tested routinely.

How often should we screen?

OFAC says the frequency "must be guided by your organization's internal policies and procedures". The Framework also expects a program to adjust rapidly when OFAC publishes list changes.

Will OFAC tell us whether a hit is a real match?

No. OFAC does not confirm potential matches or false positives. It expects a risk-based decision, documented in your records.

What is the deadline to report a blocked or rejected transaction?

10 business days, under 31 CFR 501.603 for blocked property and 501.604 for rejected transactions.
